sourceBindings.text: When someone becomes unwell in the field, your first decisions matter. Practise recognizing danger, getting the right help and giving only the assistance you are trained to provide.
Recognize injury and heat emergency warning signs, including possible heatstroke in a person who is still sweating.
Give a clear emergency report and justify which immediate actions are appropriate for the situation and your training.
Demonstrate a safe response simulation, summon help and select suitable first-aid equipment under trainer observation.

sourceBindings.text: A person trips near the farm access road. A vehicle is approaching and the person says their leg hurts.
Assess the traffic and stay out of its path. Warn others without entering an unsafe area.
Alert the supervisor and summon emergency help if the injury is serious. Give the access-road location.
Reassure the person from a safe position. Do not pull them up or test the painful leg. Follow appropriate emergency guidance.
Helping starts with scene safety; a familiar fall does not justify moving a possible fracture.

sourceBindings.text: Your partner is sweating heavily, has a headache and feels nauseated after working in the sun. The vehicle is far away. They are alert and can swallow normally.
Stop work and recognize possible heat exhaustion. Use the nearest safe shade; do not make them keep working or walk a long distance to the vehicle.
Alert the supervisor, report the location and symptoms, and arrange medical assessment. Keep someone with the person.
Loosen unnecessary clothing, cool with wet cloths on the head, neck and armpits and with fanning, and offer small sips of cool water while they remain alert and able to swallow.
If they become confused, collapse or worsen, call 123 immediately and continue cooling. Do not wait for sweating to stop and do not give drinks if swallowing is unsafe.
Observe the person continuously: heavy sweating can continue even when the situation becomes an emergency.

sourceBindings.text: A colleague falls into a shallow hidden hole. Their ankle is at an unusual angle, the pain is severe and they cannot move safely. The immediate area is otherwise safe.
Keep other people away from the hole and check for additional hazards.
Call for emergency medical help. Describe the severe pain, unusual ankle position, exact field location and safest access route. Report a suspected injury, not a confirmed diagnosis.
Keep the person still and reassured. Do not straighten the ankle, pull off footwear to inspect it or ask them to walk. Support or immobilize only as trained and directed.
If there is bleeding, provide appropriate direct-pressure care without pressing on protruding bone. Protect the person from chilling or overheating and watch for changes until help arrives.
The safe response does not depend on proving whether the injury is a sprain or fracture.

sourceBindings.text: During an authorized task, liquid fertilizer splashes into your partner's eye. The surrounding area is safe and the planned eyewash is accessible.
Begin suitable flushing immediately. Scene safety is a rapid check, not a reason to postpone washing.
Ask a helper to summon medical help and bring the product information. Explain the location, eye exposure, product if known and current condition.
Keep flushing according to product and medical guidance. Do not stop merely because 15 minutes has elapsed, and do not delay washing while searching for paperwork.
Urgent assistance and the call for help can happen together.

sourceBindings.text: You find gauze, tape, a small eyewash bottle, an emergency blanket and written contact details in the field kit.
For a deep cut, choose clean gauze for direct pressure. Tape may support a dressing when used appropriately; fetching it must not delay pressure or the call for help.
For an eye splash, start the appropriate flushing and check access to the full eyewash provision. The small bottle alone may run out too soon.
Use the written contacts and location information to make an accurate call even under stress. Select the blanket only when protection from chilling is appropriate.
Knowing why an item is needed matters more than reciting the kit inventory.

sourceBindings.text: Use role cards, clean unused equipment and a training prop. No real chemicals, deliberate heat exposure, injury, eye flushing on classmates or force on a limb. Mock calls must not dial emergency services.
Before the rehearsal, locate the safe area, communication equipment, kit and washing facilities with the trainer. Confirm the emergency number and access information for the actual location.
In a group of 3–4, read the assigned scenario and spend up to 15 minutes developing a response. Identify immediate actions, suitable protection, the emergency report and responsibilities.
Rehearse the dizzy-partner and suspected-ankle-injury cases. In the next step, rehearse the chemical-splash and airborne-hazard cases to practise all four situations.

Each learner must individually demonstrate the scene assessment, a mock emergency report, equipment selection and safe limits of assistance. Explain an eye-splash response using a prop, without actually flushing a person's eyes.
Present the group's reasoning in 2–3 minutes. Use the shared 15-minute discussion period to compare plans and correct unsafe decisions. Group participation does not replace individual evidence.
Test a communication failure: explain the agreed safe backup if mobile coverage is lost. Repeat the affected action after feedback. The trainer records what was observed and what still needs work.
A five-part emergency report with accurate scenario facts.
Individual observation of scene safety, timely help, appropriate equipment and assistance within training.
Recognition of heatstroke despite continued sweating; no drink offered when swallowing is unsafe.
No straightening or unnecessary movement of a suspected fracture; no delay to urgent eye washing in the simulation.

Every practical element must be demonstrated safely to the trainer. Stop an unsafe simulation, explain the hazard, and repeat the affected performance. Online answers or a group presentation alone cannot pass this criterion.

sourceBindings.text: For a person beside moving traffic, a confused person after heat exposure, and an eye splash, choose the first safe observation, the help to summon and an action within your training. Say what would make you stop or escalate.
Mark the danger to responders and bystanders in each scene.
Select an emergency report with location, observed condition and hazard, without inventing a diagnosis.
Choose cooling and emergency help for possible heatstroke even if the person is sweating; choose prompt appropriate eye flushing for a splash and do not delay it for cleanup.
Match a safe training-kit item to its purpose, or say why no item should be used without instruction.
Online choices rehearse reasoning only. The response simulation and equipment selection require trainer observation; no real heat, injury or chemical exposure.

sourceBindings.text: Can I explain and demonstrate an emergency response within my training?
This step covers injury and heat response. Complete the spill-response and evacuation step for the other parts of emergency preparation. Self-rating does not certify practical competence.

sourceBindings.text: Assess
Check the situation, immediate dangers and observed condition before choosing a safe response.
Alert
Summon appropriate help and communicate useful facts.
Attend
Give appropriate assistance within your training while help is arranged.
Fracture
A break or crack in a bone; a suspected fracture needs medical assessment.
Heat exhaustion
Heat-related illness involving symptoms such as heavy sweating, weakness and dizziness.
Heatstroke
A dangerous heat emergency that may include confusion, seizures or unconsciousness, with or without sweating.
SDS
Safety data sheet: product information that includes hazards and first-aid measures.
